scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance arose during the 1980s in Sweden.
It was developed as a response to a shortage of male dancers in social settings, leading to the discovery that the Swedish Bugg could be performed by three people simultaneously.
It is part of the BRR (Bugg and Rock'n'Roll) dance family.
on_screen: Map: Sweden · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social solution for a lack of partners, it is now a competitive discipline that emphasizes formation, coordination, and the creative adaptation of swing movements for a trio.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Double bugg is performed by three people, usually one man and two women.
The dancers form various patterns including lines, circles, and triangles.
A key feature is the constant changing of places between the three dancers while maintaining the swing rhythm and lead-follow connection.
Watch for Formation change, Place changing.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dynamic shifting between lines, circles, and triangles

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is mainly performed to modern pop or rock'n'roll music.
The music provides a rhythmic foundation similar to other swing-based dances like Boogie Woogie and Lindy Hop.
The pulse is 4/4.
The music is characterized by modern pop production or classic rock'n'roll arrangements, featuring a clear, driving beat suitable for athletic swing dancing.

narration: The dance is administered by the Swedish Dancesport Federation (DSF) and the World Rock'n'Roll Confederation (WRRC).
While primarily a Swedish tradition, it is recognized internationally through the World Rock'n'Roll Confederation.
Double bugg is a descendant of Bugg, which itself originated from Lindy Hop (Jitterbug).
